name: AI Insurance
blurb:
Insurance is where AI risk stops being a principle and acquires a price. An underwriter has to decide what a model failure costs, whether a coolant leak in a liquid-cooled rack is a property claim or an equipment breakdown, and whether a policy written before generative AI existed still covers what the insured is now doing with it. Those decisions are being made now, mostly quietly, and they will shape deployment more directly than most published guidance.

This hub tracks both directions. How insurers use AI in underwriting and claims, and, more consequentially for the industry, how the insurance market prices the AI and data centre buildout: property and business interruption on facilities, errors and omissions on model outputs, cyber cover for prompt injection and model extraction, intellectual property defence for training data, supply chain cover on chips and transformers, and the actuarial problem of pricing a risk with no claims history.

Ten sections, each tracking a distinct part of the value chain.

built.name: Physical Infrastructure and Property
built.detail: Property cover on the buildings themselves.

built.name: Business Interruption and Power Grid
built.detail: What a stoppage costs and who pays. Utility load shedding and throttling, contingent business interruption when a hyperscaler outage freezes downstream applications, subsea cable cuts, GPU provider service level breaches, power purchase...

built.name: Model Liability and Errors and Omissions
built.detail: Cover for what a model does. Algorithmic bias class actions in hiring, lending and tenant screening, autonomous agents executing bad transactions, diagnostic AI malpractice, hallucinated professional advice, autonomous vehicle product...

built.name: Intellectual Property and Copyright
built.detail: The training data question, priced. Copyright infringement defence for developers facing class actions, output ownership and patent invalidity, scraping under GDPR and CCPA, trade secret contamination from code entering public training...

built.name: Cyber, Data Breach and Prompt Injection
built.detail: Where cyber policy language meets attacks that did not exist when it was written.

built.name: Supply Chain, Chips and Hardware
built.detail: Cover on the physical inputs. Cargo and transit on high value GPU shipments, foundry concentration risk in Taiwan, thermal shock damage during cooling failure, transformer and switchgear lead times running to four years, secondary market...

built.detail: How a premium gets calculated for a risk with no claims history.

points.desc: RAND's September 2026 report on the insurability of AI finds a small number of carriers affirmatively covering AI losses, a growing number filing broad exclusions, and most staying silent. Silence leaves coverage untested and open to dispute. RAND calls it the hardest posture to manage because it hides both what is insured and where correlated losses are building.
points.name: Carriers have split three ways: cover, exclude, or say nothing

points.desc: RAND finds AI losses reaching technology errors and omissions, professional liability, cyber, directors and officers, commercial property and more. A single event can look like a cyber incident, a professional error and a product defect at once. Whether a loss is covered now turns on the wording of each policy, not on which policies a company holds.
points.name: AI risk does not sit in one line the way cyber does

points.desc: RAND reviewed AI forms filed in the US admitted market from the launch of ChatGPT through June 21, 2026. It found 125 forms from 60 insurers, of which 112 were exclusions and 7 were endorsements. Most exclusions sit on commercial umbrella and commercial general liability policies, and no stand alone AI policy had been filed in the admitted market.
points.name: Exclusion filings surged from the summer of 2025

points.desc: The report recommends that state insurance regulators and the NAIC develop a standard notice in which a carrier states, line by line, whether AI losses are covered, excluded or left silent. Only the format and core definitions would be standard. Carriers would keep control of their coverage terms.
points.name: RAND proposes an AI Coverage Notice

points.desc: RAND contrasts AI with cyber, where most claims are first party costs such as forensics and system repair. AI losses to date come mainly through litigation brought by others. It also notes that AI underwriting looks at governance, model validation and human oversight, where cyber underwriting looks at technical controls.
points.name: Most AI losses so far are third party claims

summary: How the insurance market prices AI and data centre risk, and how insurers use AI. Ten sections, each tracking a distinct part of the value chain, each item with its own page.
